text: Samsung Group, a South Korean multinational manufacturing conglomerate headquartered in the Samsung Town office complex in Seoul, is the largest chaebol in South Korea and, as of 2024, has the world's fifth-highest brand value. Founded in 1938 by Lee Byung-chul as a trading company named Mitsuboshi Trading Company (Samsung Sanghoe), it began with forty employees in Su-dong (now Ingyo-dong), dealing in dried fish, locally-grown groceries, and noodles. After moving its head office to Seoul in 1947, Lee was forced to leave during the Korean War and established Cheil Jedang in Pusan. In 1954, he founded Cheil Mojik, a textiles company, which became the largest woollen mill in the country at the time. The company diversified into insurance, securities, and retail. In 1947, Cho Hong-jai co-founded Samsung Mulsan Gongsa (later Samsung C&T Corporation) with Lee Byung-chul, though they later separated due to management differences. In the late 1960s, Samsung entered the electronics industry, forming divisions such as Samsung Electronics Devices, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Samsung Corning, and Samsung Semiconductor & Telecommunications, with its first product being a black-and-white television set. Lee Byung-chul also owned Tongyang Broadcasting Company (TBC), which operated from 1964 to 1980 and helped boost sales of Samsung televisions. In 1980, Samsung acquired Hanguk Jeonja Tongsin in Kumi and entered telecommunications hardware, producing over 800 million mobile phones, which were later grouped under Samsung Electronics. After Lee Byung-chul's death in 1987, the Samsung Group was divided into five business groups: Samsung Group, Shinsegae Group, CJ Group, Hansol Group, and JoongAng Group. These groups, including Shinsegae, CJ, Hansol, and JoongAng, became independent with severed payment guarantees and share-holding ties. In the 1980s, Samsung Electronics invested heavily in R&D, building plants in Portugal (1982), New York (1984), Tokyo (1985), England (1987), and Austin, Texas (1996), with over $13 billion invested in the Austin facility, making it the largest foreign investment in Texas and one of the largest single foreign investments in the U.S. In 1987, the U.S. International Trade Commission found Samsung unlawfully sold computer chips without Texas Instruments' licenses. Since 1990, Samsung has globalized its operations, with mobile phones and semiconductors becoming key income sources. The company built the Petronas Towers in Malaysia, Taipei 101 in Taiwan, and the Burj Khalifa in the UAE. In 1993, Lee Kun-hee sold off ten subsidiaries and focused operations on electronics, engineering, and chemicals. In 1996, Samsung reacquired the Sungkyunkwan University foundation. Samsung became the world's largest memory chip producer in 1992 and the second-largest chipmaker after Intel. In 1995, its textile division invested in FUBU, and it created its first liquid-crystal display screen, becoming the world's largest manufacturer of LCD panels. Sony later partnered with Samsung in 2006 to form S-LCD, a joint venture with Samsung owning 50% plus one share and Sony 50% minus one share, operating in Tanjung, South Korea, with Samsung acquiring Sony’s stake by December 26, 2011. Samsung survived the 1997 Asian financial crisis, though Samsung Motor was sold to Renault at a loss, with Renault owning 80.1% and Samsung 19.9%. Samsung manufactured aircraft from the 1980s to the 1990s, founding Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI) in 1999 through a merger of Samsung Aerospace, Daewoo Heavy Industries, and Hyundai Space and Aircraft Company, and continues to produce aircraft engines and gas turbines. In 2000, Samsung R&D opened a center in Warsaw, Poland, initially focused on set-top-box technology, later expanding to digital TV and smartphones, with the original Samsung Solstice line launched in 2008 and evolving into the Galaxy line. In 2007, former Samsung lawyer Kim Yong Chul claimed involvement in bribing and fabricating evidence for chairman Lee Kun-hee, stating that executives were used as scapegoats and that Samsung had raised secret funds through 1,000 illegally opened bank accounts, including four under his name managing 5 billion won. In 2010, Samsung announced a ten-year growth strategy including a ₩2.1 trillion commitment to biopharmaceuticals. In Q1 2012, Samsung Electronics became the world's largest mobile phone maker by unit sales, surpassing Nokia. On August 24, 2012, nine U.S. jurors ruled Samsung must pay Apple $1.05 billion in damages for patent infringement on six smartphone technologies, though Apple did not infringe on five Samsung patents; the decision led to a 7.7% drop in Samsung shares to 1,177,000 KRW and Apple's attempt to ban eight Samsung phones, which was denied. In 2013, Taiwan’s Fair Trade Commission investigated Samsung and its local advertising agency for false advertising after complaints about students being used to attack competitors in online forums; Samsung stated it had stopped such campaigns. In 2015, Samsung received more U.S. patents than any other company, with 7,679 utility patents by December 11. The Galaxy Note 7 launched on August 19, 2016, but was suspended in September due to battery defects causing fires and explosions; a new version was released, but it also had the defect, leading to a global recall on October 10, 2016, and permanent cessation of production the next day. In 2018, Samsung inaugurated the world's largest mobile manufacturing facility in Noida, India, with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and South Korean President Moon Jae-in. In 2023, Samsung announced a reduction in memory chip production due to a projected 96% decline in quarterly operating profit—down 600 million won from 14 trillion won in 2022—attributed to weak post-COVID demand and a slowing global economy, despite a 4% share increase. Samsung was the top two applicant for PCT patents in 2022 and 2023. U.S. Patent No. 9,675,229 and its European counterpart were challenged; the European patent was revoked in March 2024, and the U.S. patent lapsed in June 2025 due to non-payment of maintenance fees. Samsung has significant influence on South Korea’s economy, politics, media, and culture, being a major force behind the "Miracle on the Han River," with its affiliates producing about one-fifth of South Korea’s total exports and generating 22.4% of the country’s $1.67 trillion GDP in 2022. Critics argue that Samsung is more powerful than the South Korean president, managing legal, media, academic, and bureaucratic institutions, with one presidential candidate stating Samsung "has the government in its hands." Samsung comprises around 80 companies, operating in construction, consumer electronics, financial services, shipbuilding, medical services, and high-polymer chemicals, genetic engineering, aerospace, and nanotechnology. As of April 2011, the group included 59 unlisted and 19 listed companies, all primarily listed on the Korea Exchange. In FY 2009, Samsung reported consolidated revenues of 220 trillion KRW ($172.5 billion); in FY 2010, revenues reached 280 trillion KRW ($258 billion) with profits of 30 trillion KRW ($27.6 billion) at a KRW-USD exchange rate of 1,084.5 as of August 19, 2011; these figures do not include revenues from subsidiaries outside South Korea. In 2024, Samsung ranked first globally in the number of industrial design applications under the Hague System, with 544 applications submitted in 2023. Samsung formed the Samsung Strategy and Innovation Center (SSIC) in 2012 and Samsung NEXT in 2013 for incubation, investment, partnerships, and acquisitions; in 2017, Samsung NEXT launched a $150 million fund for early-stage software and services startups; Samsung Catalyst Fund, SSIC’s investment arm, has funded 15–20 startups annually, focusing on IoT, cloud, data storage, smart machines, smart health, and privacy and security. In 2025, Samsung Electronics launched a business support division with a dedicated mergers and acquisitions team. The basic color in the logo is blue, which Samsung has used for years.

Samsung has 544 industrial design applications globally, with 544 submitted in 2023. The company established the Samsung Strategy and Innovation Center (SSIC) in 2012 and Samsung NEXT in 2013 to support incubation, investment, partnerships, and acquisitions. In 2017, Samsung NEXT launched a USD 150 million fund for early-stage software and services startups. Samsung Catalyst Fund, SSIC’s investment arm, has funded 15 to 20 startups annually. SSIC primarily focuses on internet of things, cloud and computer data storage, smart machines, smart health, and privacy and security. In 2025, Samsung Electronics launched a business support division with a dedicated mergers and acquisitions team. Samsung’s logo features blue, which the company has used for years, symbolizing stability, reliability, and corporate social responsibility. Samsung once had an audio logo composed of the notes E♭, A♭, D♭, E♭—rising a perfect fourth to A♭, descending a perfect fifth to D♭, then ascending a major second back to E♭—produced by Musikvergnuegen and written by Walter Werzowa. This audio logo was discontinued as of 2015. In 2014, Samsung introduced the Samsung Sharp Sans font. In July 2016, Samsung unveiled SamsungOne, a typeface designed to provide a consistent visual identity across its diverse product range, from smartphones to connected TVs and refrigerators, with a focus on legibility and supporting 400 languages through over 25,000 characters. In 2013, Samsung spent an estimated $14 billion on advertising and marketing, representing 5.4% of its annual revenue—higher than any of the world’s top-20 companies by sales (Apple at 0.6%, General Motors at 3.5%). Samsung became the world’s largest advertiser in 2012, spending $4.3 billion compared to Apple’s $1 billion. Its global brand value of $39.6 billion is less than half that of Apple. In March 2008, Samsung received an investment certificate and began construction of its first mobile phone manufacturing plant in Vietnam, Samsung Electronics Vietnam (SEV) in Bac Ninh, originally with a $670 million investment, later increased to $1.5 billion, then to $2.5 billion—nearly four times the original. From 2018 to 2022, Samsung contributed over $306 billion in export revenue to Vietnam, reaching $65 billion in 2022 alone, which helped Vietnam’s total exports exceed the 700 billion USD threshold, reaching over 732 billion USD. Samsung has also deepened Vietnamese businesses’ integration into the global value chain, increasing the number of Vietnamese first- and second-tier suppliers in its supply chain from 25 in 2014 to 257 by the end of 2022. Samsung faced complaints about child labor in its supply chain from 2012 to 2015. In July 2014, Samsung terminated its contract with Shinyang Electronics after receiving a complaint about child labor violations; Samsung stated its investigation found evidence of underage workers and that it severed ties immediately under its "zero tolerance" policy. China Labor Watch (CLW) criticized HEG, a Chinese supplier, for employing underage workers in July 2014, claiming over ten children under 16 were employed, with the youngest being 14 years old; HEG denied the claims and sued CLW. CLW also alleged HEG violated overtime rules, stating a female college student was paid standard wages despite working four hours of overtime daily, which violates Chinese law requiring 1.5 to 2.0 times standard wages. Samsung claimed its onsite investigation found no evidence of child labor, and CLW stated the workers were dismissed before Samsung’s investigators arrived. CLW also claimed HEG violated overtime rules for adult workers. In 2020, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute accused at least 82 major brands, including Samsung, of being linked to alleged forced Uyghur labor in Xinjiang. Samsung maintains a no-union policy and has engaged in union-busting activities worldwide. A union sued Samsung for allegedly stealing the corpse of a dead worker. On 6 May 2020, Samsung vice chairman Lee Jae-yong apologized for union-busting scandals. Kim Yong-chul, former head of Samsung’s legal department, and the Catholic Priests Association for Justice uncovered Lee Kun-hee’s slush fund on 29 October 2007, presenting a list of 30 artworks purchased by the Lee family with slush funds, stored in a warehouse in southern Seoul, along with documents on bribes to prosecutors, judges, lawmakers, and tax collectors using thousands of borrowed-named bank accounts. Lee Kun-hee was sentenced to three years in prison with five years probation and fined ₩11 billion (US$9.62 million), but on 29 December 2009, South Korean President Lee Myung-bak pardoned him, citing the intent to allow him to remain on the International Olympic Committee. Kim Yong-chul published the book Thinking about Samsung in 2010, detailing Samsung’s behavior and how the company lobbied government officials, including court officials, prosecutors, and tax service officials, to transfer management rights to Lee Jae-yong. In July 2016, investigative journal KCIJ-Newstapa released a video allegedly showing Samsung chairman Lee Kun-hee paying prostitutes for sex acts, filmed on five separate occasions between December 2011 and June 2013 at his residence and a secret rental home. Police detained six suspects for taking the videos without Lee Kun-hee’s knowledge; investigators claimed the suspects extorted ₩500 million (US$437,082.04) from Samsung, a claim denied by Samsung representatives. One suspect, surnamed Seon, was a former executive of CJ CheilJedang, a former Samsung Group company that separated in 1993. Lee Kun-hee’s older brother, Lee Jay-hyun, is the chairman of CJ CheilJedang, and the two had a heated rivalry. Rumors circulated that Lee Jay-hyun coordinated the scandal against his younger brother, but prosecutors found no sufficient evidence of CJ leadership involvement. On 12 April 2018, a former CJ CheilJedang employee was sentenced to four years and six months in prison for blackmail and intimidation. While prosecutors considered investigating Lee Kun-hee for sex trafficking, no charges were pursued, likely due to his health; Lee Kun-hee suffered a heart attack in 2014 and remained in a coma until his death in 2020. In February 2017, de facto Samsung leader Lee Jae-yong was arrested for bribery, embezzlement, hiding assets overseas, and perjury. It was alleged he paid ₩43 billion (US$37.59 million) to a close friend of President Park Geun-hye in exchange for government approval of a merger between two Samsung affiliates. He was initially convicted and sentenced to five years in prison, but the sentence was suspended and reduced to two and a half years after a year in prison by the Seoul High Court. In a 2021 retrial, Lee was sentenced to two and a half years in prison. He was released early after serving 10 months in August 2021 as part of South Korea’s Liberation Day clemency tradition. In August 2022, Lee received a presidential pardon, supported by 70% of the Korean public according to local polls. Special prosecutors investigating the 2016 South Korean political scandal revealed that the Blue House received funds from South Korea’s four largest chaebols—Samsung, Hyundai Motor Group, SK Group, and LG Group—to finance pro-government demonstrations by conservative and far-right groups such as the Korean Parent Federation and the Moms Brigade. On 19 October 2011, Samsung was fined €145,727,000 for participating in a DRAM price cartel involving ten companies from 1 July 1998 to 15 June 2002. The companies received a 10% reduction for cooperating with investigators; Samsung paid 90% of its share, while Micron avoided payment due to early disclosure. In Canada, during 1999, DRAM manufacturers including Samsung conspired to fix prices, investigated in 2002, and the price-fixing ended due to a recession; in 2014, the Canadian government reopened the case and found sufficient evidence, leading to a $120 million settlement, with $40 million as a fine and $80 million to be returned to Canadians who purchased electronics from April 1999 to June 2002. In Australia in 2022, the competition and consumer commission fined Samsung AU$14 million for misleading water resistance claims for over 3.1 million smartphones. Between 2016 and 2018, Samsung advertised Galaxy S7, S7 Edge, A5, A7, S8, S8 Plus, and Note 8 devices as water-resistant, but after user complaints about corrosion from water exposure, the ACCC determined the claims were misleading and proceeded with the fine. Since 2024, a spyware called Landfall has been active on Samsung Galaxy phones in the Middle East, including in Iraq, Iran, Turkey, and Morocco, capable of accessing complete user data such as photos, sounds, and calls without user interaction, distributed via WhatsApp and infecting many phones over a year.
